title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
setting: The Italian states of the 1490s and 1500s, with examples drawn from Rome, Greece, Persia and the Bible
lengthNote: Twenty-six short chapters and a dedication; W. K. Marriott’s 1908 English translation, printed here with his introduction
openingLine: All states, all powers, that have held and hold rule over men have been and are either republics or principalities.
summary: A dismissed Florentine civil servant, tortured on suspicion of conspiracy and living on a farm outside the city, writes a short book on how principalities are won, held and lost, and addresses it to the family that sacked him. It argues from cases rather than principles: Cesare Borgia, who did everything right and fell; Agathocles, who won a kingdom by murder and no glory; Louis XII, who made five errors and a sixth. Its scandal is not that it recommends cruelty but that it asks what cruelty is for, and answers coolly. The closing chapter drops the analytic voice for a plea to drive the foreigners out of Italy.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Prince, translated by W. K. Marriott
sourceText.note: References give the chapter number; the dedication to Lorenzo de’ Medici stands before Chapter 1. Marriott renders virtù variously as ‘ability’, ‘valour’ and ‘talent’, and the quotations keep his choices.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Machiavelli describes the ‘small work on Principalities’ in a letter to Francesco Vettori of 13 December 1513, months after his release from prison.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: In Rome by Antonio Blado, five years after the author’s death; the book had circulated in manuscript for nearly twenty years.

atAGlance.label: Dedicated to
atAGlance.note: The dedication was first intended for his uncle Giuliano; there is no evidence Lorenzo read it.

atAGlance.label: Chief example
atAGlance.note: Duke Valentino, whom Machiavelli watched at close range as Florence’s envoy in 1502–3, fills Chapter 7.

atAGlance.label: This translation
atAGlance.note: Made for Everyman’s Library, and aiming, in Marriott’s words, at ‘an exact literal rendering’ rather than a fluent paraphrase.

structure.label: Dedication and Chapters 1–5
structure.title: What kinds of principality there are, and how new ones are held
structure.summary: A dedication that offers the book as the only thing its author owns, then a taxonomy: hereditary states, mixed states, states used to a prince and states used to freedom. Chapter 3 is the longest and the most practical, using Louis XII’s conduct in Italy to derive rules for holding what one has seized, including the advice that men must be either well treated or crushed. Chapter 5 concludes that a city accustomed to liberty is safest destroyed.

scenes.title: The gift
scenes.summary: Machiavelli sends the knowledge of great men’s actions, acquired by long experience, as the most precious thing he has.

scenes.title: Louis and his errors
scenes.summary: Five mistakes and a sixth; the general rule that he who makes another powerful is ruined.

scenes.title: Free cities
scenes.summary: Pisa after a hundred years of Florentine rule still rallies to the name of liberty.

structure.label: Chapters 6–9
structure.title: New princes: by ability, by fortune, by crime, by the people
structure.summary: Four ways a private man becomes a prince. Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus owed fortune nothing but opportunity, and all armed prophets have conquered. Cesare Borgia rose on his father’s fortune, did everything a wise man could, and fell with it; his execution of Remirro de Orco in the square at Cesena is the book’s most famous case. Agathocles won Syracuse by massacre and is denied glory for it. The civil prince, raised by the people or the nobles, learns which of the two he can afford to disappoint.

scenes.title: Armed prophets
scenes.summary: The founders, and Savonarola as the unarmed one who was ruined when the multitude stopped believing.

scenes.title: Cesare Borgia
scenes.summary: The Romagna pacified by a cruel minister, and the minister left in two pieces in the piazza.

scenes.title: Agathocles
scenes.summary: Cruelties well used and badly used; empire without glory.

scenes.title: The civil principality
scenes.summary: The people ask only not to be oppressed; the nobles want to oppress.

structure.label: Chapters 10–14
structure.title: Arms: mercenaries, auxiliaries and a prince’s own
structure.summary: The middle of the book is about soldiers. Good laws rest on good arms; mercenaries are useless and dangerous, and Italy’s ruin is laid at the door of the condottieri who fought for pay and avoided battle. Auxiliaries, borrowed from a stronger power, are worse. A prince should study nothing but war, walk his own country to learn its ground, and read the histories of great captains.

scenes.title: Mercenaries
scenes.summary: Valiant before friends, cowardly before enemies; the Italian captains who made war bloodless and lost Italy.

scenes.title: The art of war
scenes.summary: No other aim or thought for a prince than war and its discipline.

structure.label: Chapters 15–19
structure.title: How a prince should behave: the chapters that made the name
structure.summary: Machiavelli announces that he will follow the real truth of the matter rather than the imagination of it, and then works through the virtues a prince is praised for, asking which he can afford. Generosity ruins; a reputation for cruelty may be merciful; it is safer to be feared than loved, provided one is not hated; a prince must be both fox and lion, and need not keep faith when keeping it would hurt him, so long as he appears to. Chapter 19 tests all this against the Roman emperors, and finds that only Severus managed both soldiers and people.

scenes.title: The real truth
scenes.summary: Imagined republics set aside for how men actually live.

scenes.title: Feared or loved
scenes.summary: Men forget a father’s death sooner than a lost patrimony.

scenes.title: The fox and the lion
scenes.summary: Everyone sees what you appear to be; few know what you are.

structure.label: Chapters 20–23
structure.title: Fortresses, reputation, ministers and flatterers
structure.summary: Practical chapters on the machinery of rule. The best fortress is not to be hated by the people. A prince is respected for great enterprises and for declaring himself a true friend or a downright enemy, never a neutral. He is judged by the men he keeps around him, and he must let a few wise men tell him the truth without letting everyone do so.

scenes.title: Fortresses
scenes.summary: Castles that protect a prince from his people are a sign he needs protecting from them.

scenes.title: Neutrality
scenes.summary: The Roman legate to the Achaeans: not to interfere is to be the guerdon of the conqueror.

scenes.title: Flatterers
scenes.summary: Courts are full of them, because men are so self-complacent in their own affairs.

structure.label: Chapters 24–26
structure.title: Why Italy’s princes lost their states, what Fortune governs, and an exhortation
structure.summary: The princes of Italy lost their states through their own faults, not fortune’s. Fortune is the arbiter of half our actions and leaves the other half to us; she is a raging river that can be banked in fair weather, and a woman who favours the impetuous. The last chapter abandons analysis for an appeal to the Medici to seize the moment and free Italy from the barbarians, ending with lines of Petrarch.

scenes.title: Fortune
scenes.summary: Half our actions, a river in flood, and the case of Julius II, who succeeded by never being cautious.

scenes.title: The exhortation
scenes.summary: Italy waits for a liberator; to all of us this barbarous dominion stinks.

characters.name: The prince
characters.role: The book’s addressee and its subject: a new ruler holding a state he was not born to
characters.summary: Not a person but a position, and the book keeps him deliberately abstract so that any reader can occupy the chair. He is assumed to want one thing, to hold his state, and every chapter asks what that wanting costs. Marriott’s ‘ability’ is Machiavelli’s virtù: not goodness but capacity, the power to see an opportunity and to act before it closes.
characters.clue: Never named, he is told to study nothing but war, to be a fox and a lion, and to seem merciful, faithful and religious whether or not he is.

relationships.label: governed by half, master of the rest

characters.name: Cesare Borgia, Duke Valentino
characters.role: Son of Pope Alexander VI; conqueror of the Romagna; the book’s chief modern example
characters.summary: Machiavelli watched him as Florence’s envoy and never quite recovered. Chapter 7 presents him as the man who rose by his father’s fortune and laid every foundation a wise prince could: he pacified the Romagna with a cruel minister and then displayed the minister’s body, killed his rivals, won Rome, and prepared for his father’s death. He fell anyway, ill at the wrong moment and allowing the wrong cardinal to become pope, and the book calls that fortune’s extraordinary malignity.
characters.clue: He pacified a province with a cruel minister and then left the minister in two pieces in a piazza; he did everything right and fell when his father died.

relationships.label: held up as an example to

characters.name: Agathocles of Syracuse
characters.role: A potter’s son who made himself king by massacring the senate; the book’s example of power won by crime
characters.summary: He rose through the army, assembled the citizens and senators of Syracuse as if to consult them, and had them killed; he then held the city against Carthage and was never conspired against. Machiavelli admits his courage and his ability, and refuses him glory: killing fellow citizens and betraying friends may gain empire but not honour. The distinction is one the book is often accused of not making.
characters.clue: A potter’s son who called the senators of his city to a meeting and had them murdered, and whom the book allows empire but not glory.

characters.name: Fortune
characters.role: The power that governs half of human affairs
characters.summary: Personified as a river in flood and as a woman, Fortune is the book’s one recurring antagonist. She raised Cesare Borgia and broke him; she made Julius II succeed by suiting his impetuous temper; she favours the bold and the young. Machiavelli’s answer to her is preparation, banks built in fair weather, and a readiness to change one’s nature with the times, which he admits almost nobody has.
characters.clue: A river that can be banked in dry weather and a woman who prefers the impetuous; she takes half of everything and leaves the rest to us.

characters.name: Louis XII of France
characters.role: The king who took Milan twice and lost it twice; the example of Chapter 3
characters.summary: Machiavelli met him on embassy and uses him as the textbook case of how to lose a conquest: he destroyed the minor powers, aggrandised the Church, brought Spain into Italy, did not settle in the country and sent no colonies, and then committed a sixth error by ruining Venice. The chapter ends with Machiavelli telling Cardinal Rouen that the French do not understand statecraft.
characters.clue: A king who quickly occupied Milan and as quickly lost it, and whose five errors and a sixth fill the longest chapter.

relationships.label: helped Alexander and so made him possible

characters.name: Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus
characters.summary: The highest examples of new princes who owed fortune nothing but opportunity: an enslaved people, a discontented nation, an abandoned child, a scattered city. Machiavelli sets Moses among them with a careful bow to God and then treats him as a founder like the others, which was noticed. Savonarola, whom Machiavelli had watched fall in Florence, is their unarmed opposite.
characters.clue: Four founders who needed only an opportunity, and whose armed success is set against a Florentine friar who was ruined when the crowd stopped believing.

characters.name: The people
characters.role: The many, whose goodwill is the only fortress
characters.summary: Machiavelli’s people want not to be oppressed, which is a smaller and safer demand than the nobles’ wish to oppress. They judge by the eye rather than the hand, are taken by what a thing seems to be and what comes of it, and are the reason a prince must avoid hatred above all. The book’s republican sympathies show through here more than anywhere.
characters.clue: They ask only not to be oppressed, judge by what they see, and are the one thing a prince cannot afford to be hated by.

characters.name: The nobles
characters.role: The few, who wish to command and consider the prince their equal
characters.summary: A prince raised by the nobles has many around him who think themselves his equals and cannot be managed; a prince raised by the people stands alone and is obeyed. The nobles can be made and unmade daily, Machiavelli says, which is the book’s cool view of an aristocracy from a man born into one.
characters.clue: They want to oppress, think themselves the prince’s equals, and can be made and unmade at his pleasure.

relationships.label: a danger and an instrument to

themes.name: Holding power
themes.summary: The book is about keeping rather than getting: nearly every chapter turns on the difference between a state that is easy to take and hard to hold, and the reverse. Machiavelli’s measure of success is durability, which is why Agathocles’ long, secure reign disturbs him more than a tyrant’s fall would.
themes.development: Chapter 2 sets the hereditary prince as the baseline; Chapters 6–9 examine four ways of starting from nothing; Chapter 24 explains why the princes of Italy could not keep what they had.

themes.name: Fortune and ability
themes.summary: Virtù and fortuna are the book’s two forces, and Machiavelli’s proportion is exact: half and half, or a little less for fortune. The argument is not fatalist, since banks can be built, but it is bleak about temperament, because a man who could change his nature to suit the times would always prosper, and no man can.
themes.development: Fortune appears in the dedication as the author’s own malignant fate; Chapter 7 shows her raising and breaking Borgia; Chapter 25 states the theory.

themes.name: Cruelty and mercy
themes.summary: The book distinguishes cruelties by their use, not their kind: applied at one blow and not persisted in, they secure a state; renewed and multiplied, they lose it. A prince who keeps his subjects united by a few executions is more merciful than one whose softness lets disorder spread. This is the argument that made the author’s name a synonym for wickedness, and it is made with unusual care.
themes.development: Chapter 8 sorts severities into well and badly used; Chapter 17 argues that Borgia’s cruelty was mercy to the Romagna; Chapter 19 tests the claim on the Roman emperors.

themes.name: Appearance and reality
themes.summary: A prince need not have the virtues but must seem to have them, because everyone sees and few touch. The argument is about audiences: the many judge by results and by show, and the few who know better cannot stand against the many. Chapter 18 is where the book comes closest to saying that politics is performance.
themes.development: Introduced in Chapter 15 as the gap between how men live and how they ought to; made a rule of conduct in Chapter 18; applied to Ferdinand of Aragon, the pious deceiver, in Chapter 21.

themes.name: Arms and law
themes.summary: Good laws cannot exist without good arms, and a prince’s own arms are the only kind worth having. The middle chapters are the most concrete policy in the book, born of Machiavelli’s own attempt to give Florence a citizen militia, and they blame the mercenary captains for an Italy that could be overrun by anyone who came.
themes.development: Announced as the foundation of all states in Chapter 12; mercenaries and auxiliaries dismissed in Chapters 12–13; war made the prince’s only study in Chapter 14.

themes.name: Italy
themes.summary: The analytic voice breaks in the last chapter, where the divided peninsula is a body waiting to be healed and the French and Spanish are barbarians whose dominion stinks. The exhortation gives the whole book a purpose it had seemed to lack: the rules were for a prince who would use them to unite Italy, and the Medici were being asked to be him.
themes.development: Present as the ruin caused by mercenaries in Chapter 12, as Louis XII’s conquest in Chapter 3, and as the object of the plea in Chapter 26.

techniques.name: Argument by example
techniques.definition: Reasoning from named cases, ancient and recent, rather than from principles, so that the conclusion is the pattern the cases make.
techniques.inThisBook: Every rule is derived from somebody: Louis XII for holding a conquest, Borgia for the new prince, Agathocles for crime, Severus for managing soldiers. The method lets Machiavelli claim he is only reporting what has worked.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Balancing opposed terms against each other inside one line.
techniques.inThisBook: Feared or loved, fox or lion, arms or prayers, ability or fortune: the chapters are built on pairs, and the argument usually ends by choosing one and then qualifying the choice.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.inThisBook: The book is quoted in single sentences because it writes them: men forget a father’s death sooner than a lost patrimony; war is not avoided but put off to another’s advantage.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: The dedication and the last chapter speak to Lorenzo de’ Medici as ‘your Magnificence’ and ‘your illustrious house’, framing a treatise as a petition from a man who wants his job back.

techniques.name: Extended metaphor
techniques.definition: A comparison sustained across a passage until it does the arguing.
techniques.inThisBook: Fortune as a river in flood, the state as a patient with hectic fever, the prince as Chiron’s pupil who is half beast: the images carry arguments the plain prose refuses to make openly.

techniques.name: Register
techniques.definition: The level and tone of the language, and the effect of changing it.
techniques.inThisBook: Twenty-five chapters of dry classification, then an exhortation with rhetorical questions and a poem; the shift in Chapter 26 is the book’s one emotional event.

quotations.context: The last sentence of the dedication to Lorenzo de’ Medici.
quotations.analysis: The book’s last chapter will tell Lorenzo how to master fortune; its first page shows the author failing to. ‘Unmeritedly’ is doing quiet work, since Machiavelli had been imprisoned and tortured by the family he is writing to, and the sentence asks them to look down from a summit he is offering to help them climb.
quotations.text: And if your Magnificence from the summit of your greatness will sometimes turn your eyes to these lower regions, you will see how unmeritedly I suffer a great and continued malignity of fortune.

quotations.context: Drawn from the discussion of colonies, which injure a few people completely and leave the rest untouched.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a rule about revenge dressed as a rule about treatment: the reason not to do light injuries is that their victims survive to repay them. Marriott’s ‘crushed’ is blunt for a verb Machiavelli uses almost tenderly, and the calm of the syntax is the scandal.
quotations.text: men ought either to be well treated or crushed, because they can avenge themselves of lighter injuries, of more serious ones they cannot; therefore the injury that is to be done to a man ought to be of such a kind that one does not stand in fear of revenge.

quotations.context: On the Romans, who fought Philip and Antiochus in Greece so as not to fight them in Italy.
quotations.analysis: The grammar denies the reader the choice the sentence seems to offer: war is not a thing one avoids or accepts but a thing one times. The phrase returns later in the chapter against Louis XII, who yielded the Romagna ‘to avoid war’, and it is one of the book’s few claims stated as a law.
quotations.text: war is not to be avoided, but is only to be put off to the advantage of others

quotations.context: The general rule with which Chapter 3 ends, after Louis XII has made the Church and Spain great in Italy.
quotations.analysis: The rule is derived from a conversation Machiavelli reports having had with Cardinal Rouen, and the sentence explains its own mechanism: power given is power that remembers where it came from and distrusts the giver. It is the chapter’s summary of Louis, and it also describes the author’s relationship to the Medici.
quotations.text: he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined; because that predominancy has been brought about either by astuteness or else by force, and both are distrusted by him who has been raised to power.

quotations.context: On why founders have difficulty acquiring a state and ease in keeping it.
quotations.analysis: Three superlatives build the sentence up and then it explains itself with an asymmetry: enemies who are certain against defenders who are lukewarm. The passage is quoted by reformers of every kind, usually without the next paragraph, which says the remedy is to be armed.
quotations.text: there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things, because the innovator has for enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new.

quotations.context: The conclusion of the argument about whether innovators can rely on prayers or must use force.
quotations.analysis: ‘Prophets’ is the surprising noun: the founders in view are Moses and Romulus, and the sentence puts religion and force in the same hand. The next paragraph names Savonarola, whom Machiavelli had watched preach and then burn, so the maxim is autobiography as well as history.
quotations.text: Hence it is that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed.

quotations.context: Cesare Borgia, having used Remirro de Orco to pacify the Romagna by terror, disposes of him.
quotations.analysis: Two sentences of narrative and one of effect, and the effect has two halves that should not go together: satisfied and dismayed. Machiavelli is describing a piece of political theatre and admiring its economy, since the block and the knife tell the people who was responsible for the cruelty and who ended it without a word being said.
quotations.text: Under this pretence he took Ramiro, and one morning caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side. The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.

quotations.context: The judgment on Agathocles, after an admiring account of his rise.
quotations.analysis: The sentence withholds one word, glory, after granting everything else, and the list of what it will not call talent is a list of the things Chapter 18 will shortly permit. Readers who think the book has no morality tend to skip this line; readers who think it has one tend to lean on it harder than it can bear.
quotations.text: Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow-citizens, to deceive friends, to be without faith, without mercy, without religion; such methods may gain empire, but not glory.

quotations.context: Explaining how Agathocles could hold Syracuse for years after his massacre.
quotations.analysis: The parenthesis, ‘if of evil it is possible to speak well’, is the book’s conscience appearing for a clause and withdrawing. The criterion that follows is entirely practical, one blow and no repetition, and it is the same test the Borgia chapter has just applied to Remirro de Orco.
quotations.text: Those may be called properly used, if of evil it is possible to speak well, that are applied at one blow and are necessary to one’s security

quotations.context: On the civil principality, which a private citizen reaches by the favour of either the people or the nobles.
quotations.analysis: The reason given is not moral but managerial: the nobles ‘consider themselves his equals’, and a prince cannot rule men who think that. The argument prefers the people because they want less, and it is the nearest the book comes to explaining why a republican wrote a handbook for princes.
quotations.text: He who obtains sovereignty by the assistance of the nobles maintains himself with more difficulty than he who comes to it by the aid of the people, because the former finds himself with many around him who consider themselves his equals, and because of this he can neither rule nor manage them to his liking.

quotations.context: The opening of the chapters on soldiers.
quotations.analysis: The sentence begins as a pair and ends as a hierarchy: laws depend on arms, and the converse is asserted as if it followed. Machiavelli then announces he will leave the laws out, which is the book’s method in miniature, since it always takes the harder foundation and lets the softer one be inferred.
quotations.text: The chief foundations of all states, new as well as old or composite, are good laws and good arms; and as there cannot be good laws where the state is not well armed, it follows that where they are well armed they have good laws.

quotations.context: The verdict on hired soldiers, from a man who had tried to replace them in Florence with a citizen militia.
quotations.analysis: The adjectives come in a rush and the last pair is the sting: valiant before friends, cowardly before enemies. This is policy rather than theory. Machiavelli had spent years raising Florentine troops, and the passage that follows blames the condottieri for an Italy that any invader could cross.
quotations.text: Mercenaries and auxiliaries are useless and dangerous; and if one holds his state based on these arms, he will stand neither firm nor safe; for they are disunited, ambitious, and without discipline, unfaithful, valiant before friends, cowardly before enemies

quotations.context: The opening sentence of the chapter on the prince’s duty in the matter of arms.
quotations.analysis: Three negatives clear the ground before the one permitted object appears, and ‘study’ makes war an academic subject as much as a practice. The chapter goes on to recommend hunting, map-reading and the lives of great captains, which is the Renaissance humanist’s curriculum with the humanities removed.
quotations.text: A prince ought to have no other aim or thought, nor select anything else for his study, than war and its rules and discipline

quotations.context: Machiavelli explaining why his chapters on conduct will depart from everyone else’s.
quotations.analysis: The imagined republics are Plato’s and the mirror-for-princes tradition’s, and the sentence dismisses both in a subordinate clause. ‘So far distant’ measures the gap the rest of the book will work in, and the claim to be describing rather than prescribing is what lets the following chapters say what they say.
quotations.text: for many have pictured republics and principalities which in fact have never been known or seen, because how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live

quotations.context: The opening of the chapter on cruelty and clemency.
quotations.analysis: ‘Considered’ is the hinge: the sentence separates the reputation from the result and then lists the results as if they were the answer to the reputation. The Romagna, Machiavelli goes on to say, had been left in disorder by softer rulers, so that the argument is not that cruelty is good but that mercy can be the crueller policy.
quotations.text: Cesare Borgia was considered cruel; notwithstanding, his cruelty reconciled the Romagna, unified it, and restored it to peace and loyalty.

quotations.context: The answer to the question whether it is better to be loved or feared.
quotations.analysis: The famous half of the sentence is preceded by a wish for both and followed by a condition, and the conditions keep coming in the next paragraph: fear without hatred, hands off property and women. What is usually quoted as a doctrine is written as a fallback, and the reason given is about men rather than princes, that they are fickle and turn when need approaches.
quotations.text: It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.

quotations.context: The condition attached to being feared: a prince may kill for cause, but must not take property.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built so that the comparison arrives as a clinching reason rather than a shock, and the observation about human nature is offered without comment. Machiavelli adds at once that pretexts for confiscation are never wanting, which turns the maxim into advice about habit: robbery, once begun, finds its own justifications.
quotations.text: above all things he must keep his hands off the property of others, because men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony.

quotations.context: From the chapter on how princes should keep faith, after the fable of Achilles taught by the centaur Chiron.
quotations.analysis: ‘Compelled knowingly to adopt the beast’ concedes the objection before the animals appear, and then the two animals are chosen for their weaknesses rather than their strengths: the lion for what it cannot see, the fox for what it cannot fight. Those who rely on the lion alone, the passage adds, do not understand what they are about, which is the book’s general complaint against the merely brave.
quotations.text: A prince, therefore, being compelled knowingly to adopt the beast, ought to choose the fox and the lion; because the lion cannot defend himself against snares and the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. Therefore, it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves.

quotations.context: On why a prince need not possess the virtues so long as he appears to.
quotations.analysis: The second person is unusual in the book and makes the reader the prince being looked at. The sentence continues: the few who know dare not oppose the many, who have the state to defend them, so that appearance is protected by the very institution it deceives.
quotations.text: Everyone sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are

quotations.context: The close of Chapter 18, on how a prince is judged.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence behind the phrase ‘the end justifies the means’, and it does not say that. It says the means will be considered honest, a claim about judgment rather than justice, and the reason offered is that the vulgar are taken by appearances and results. The book describes a verdict without endorsing it, which is harder to quote.
quotations.text: let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody

quotations.context: After the example of the castle of Milan, which made more trouble for the Sforzas than any disorder in the state.
quotations.analysis: The chapter has praised fortresses as a custom and then dismantled the praise with examples, and the conclusion turns a building into a relationship. Marriott’s introduction says Machiavelli drew the lesson from Caterina Sforza at Forlì; it is one of the few places where the book’s advice and its sympathy for the governed coincide.
quotations.text: For this reason the best possible fortress is⁠—not to be hated by the people, because, although you may hold the fortresses, yet they will not save you if the people hate you, for there will never be wanting foreigners to assist a people who have taken arms against you. It has not been seen in our times that such fortresses have been of use to any prince, unless to the Countess of Forli,43 when the Count Girolamo, her consort, was killed; for by that means she was able to withstand the popular attack and wait for assistance from Milan, and thus recover her state; and the posture of affairs was such at that time that the foreigners could not assist the people.

quotations.context: On what makes a prince esteemed, after the example of Ferdinand of Aragon.
quotations.analysis: ‘Without any reservation’ is the operative phrase, and the chapter supports it with a Roman legate’s speech to the Achaeans: the neutral becomes the prize of whoever wins. The advice is aimed at Florence, which had spent Machiavelli’s career trying to stay friends with France without offending the Pope.
quotations.text: A prince is also respected when he is either a true friend or a downright enemy, that is to say, when, without any reservation, he declares himself in favour of one party against the other; which course will always be more advantageous than standing neutral

quotations.context: The opening of the chapter on a prince’s servants.
quotations.analysis: A prince cannot be inspected, so his ministers are read as his handwriting, and the sentence makes choosing them the first act of judgment anyone will see. The author was a servant of state looking for a master, and the chapter that follows describes the ideal minister as a man who never thinks of himself, which is a job application.
quotations.text: And the first opinion which one forms of a prince, and of his understanding, is by observing the men he has around him

quotations.context: On the danger courts are full of, and the difficulty of guarding against it.
quotations.analysis: The sentence poses a dilemma and refuses to solve it in the same breath: the only cure for flattery is licensed truth-telling, and licensed truth-telling costs respect. The next paragraph proposes a third course, a few wise men who may speak only when asked, which is the book’s general shape: an impossible pair of alternatives and a narrow path between.
quotations.text: Because there is no other way of guarding oneself from flatterers except letting men understand that to tell you the truth does not offend you; but when everyone may tell you the truth, respect for you abates.

quotations.context: The theory of fortune, stated after Machiavelli admits he is half inclined to think everything is governed by chance.
quotations.analysis: The motive comes before the finding: ‘not to extinguish our free will’ is a wish, and the proportion is what the wish allows. The sentence goes on, in the text, to give the other half to us ‘or perhaps a little less’, and that downward adjustment is the most honest thing in the chapter. The book wants free will to have half and suspects it has less.
quotations.text: Nevertheless, not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions

quotations.context: The image Machiavelli uses for Fortune, before arguing that men can build defences in fair weather.
quotations.analysis: The verbs pile up, overflows, sweeping, bearing, flies, yield, so that the sentence itself floods. The image is chosen because it has an answer: rivers can be banked, and the chapter’s point is that Italy, unlike Germany, Spain and France, is a country without dykes, which is a way of blaming rulers for what they call fate.
quotations.text: one of those raging rivers, which when in flood overflows the plains, sweeping away trees and buildings, bearing away the soil from place to place; everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it

quotations.context: The conclusion of the chapter on fortune, after the example of Julius II, who succeeded by impetuosity.
quotations.analysis: The sentence begins with a modest ‘for my part’ and ends in violence, and the image has been argued about ever since. What is often missed is the premise that precedes it: mankind is steadfast in its ways and fortune changes, so the bold man wins not because he is right but because the times more often favour him. The passage is a counsel of despair wearing the face of confidence.
quotations.text: For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly.

quotations.context: From the exhortation to the Medici to liberate Italy, the last chapter of the book.
quotations.analysis: Four rhetorical questions and then a sentence with a smell in it, in a book that has been odourless for twenty-five chapters. The shift of register is the point: the analytic voice has been in the service of this plea all along, and ‘to all of us’ is the first time the author has counted himself among a people rather than among observers.
quotations.text: What door would be closed to him? Who would refuse obedience to him? What envy would hinder him? What Italian would refuse him homage? To all of us this barbarous dominion stinks.

timeline.label: Niccolò Machiavelli born in Florence
timeline.detail: On 3 May, the son of a lawyer of the old Florentine nobility, in the Florence of Lorenzo the Magnificent.

timeline.label: Charles VIII invades Italy; the Medici are expelled
timeline.detail: The French invasion begins the wars the book describes, and Florence becomes a republic under Savonarola’s influence.

timeline.label: Savonarola burned; Machiavelli enters the Chancery
timeline.detail: The unarmed prophet of Chapter 6 is executed in May, and Machiavelli becomes Secretary to the Second Chancery in June.

timeline.label: Machiavelli on embassy to Cesare Borgia
timeline.detail: He follows the Duke through the Romagna and is at Imola and Senigallia; the material of Chapter 7 is gathered at first hand.

timeline.label: Alexander VI dies; Julius II elected; Borgia falls
timeline.detail: The pope’s death and his son’s illness bring down the state the book calls a model.

timeline.label: The Medici return to Florence
timeline.detail: The republic falls in September and Machiavelli is dismissed from office in November.

timeline.label: Imprisoned, tortured, released; The Prince written
timeline.detail: Suspected of conspiracy, he is put to the strappado, freed in the amnesty for Leo X’s election, and retires to Sant’Andrea in Percussina; his letter to Vettori of 13 December describes the ‘small work on Principalities’.

timeline.label: Machiavelli dies
timeline.detail: On 22 June, weeks after the Medici were driven out again following the Sack of Rome, without regaining office.

timeline.label: First printed edition
timeline.detail: Antonio Blado in Rome, with papal privilege; a Florentine edition by Giunta the same year.

timeline.label: Placed on the Index of Prohibited Books
timeline.detail: Machiavelli’s works are banned entire in the first Roman Index.

timeline.label: First English printed translation
timeline.detail: Edward Dacres’s version, though the book had been known in England in Italian and manuscript for decades.

timeline.label: W. K. Marriott’s translation
timeline.detail: Made for Everyman’s Library; the text of the Astor edition and of the quotations here.

places.name: Florence
places.note: The republic Machiavelli served and the Medici city he wrote for.

places.name: Sant’Andrea in Percussina
places.note: The farm south of Florence where, in his ‘noble court dress’, he wrote the book in the evenings of 1513.

places.name: Rome
places.note: The papacy of Alexander VI and Julius II, and the city where the book was first printed in 1532.

places.name: Cesena
places.note: Where Cesare Borgia left Remirro de Orco in two pieces in the piazza.

places.name: Milan
places.note: Taken and lost twice by Louis XII; the Sforza castle is the book’s example of a fortress that harms its owner.

places.name: Syracuse
places.note: Agathocles’ city, and Hiero’s, the two Sicilian examples of rising from a private station.

criticalViews.summary: The reading the book’s name records: that it teaches rulers to lie, kill and dissemble, and that its calm is the calm of a man who has stopped caring. Elizabethan drama’s ‘Machiavel’ and the Index of 1559 both belong to this tradition.
criticalViews.counter: The book denies Agathocles glory, tells the prince to keep his hands off his subjects’ property and women, and calls the people the only fortress; a manual of tyranny would not bother.

criticalViews.summary: Because the Discourses on Livy praise republics, and because The Prince ends by demanding the liberation of Italy, some readers since Rousseau have taken the book as satire or as a trap, exposing to the people what princes do.
criticalViews.counter: The letter to Vettori shows Machiavelli hoping the book would get him employed by the Medici; irony is a poor way to apply for a job.

criticalViews.summary: The most common modern view: the book separates politics from ethics as a field of study, argues from evidence rather than authority, and asks what works. Its scandal is method, not morals.
criticalViews.counter: Its examples are selected to fit and its rules contradict one another, as Chapter 25 half admits; it is less a science than a set of hard cases argued by a brilliant advocate.

essayQuestions.question: ‘It is much safer to be feared than loved.’ How far does The Prince actually recommend cruelty?
plan: Quote the sentence in full, with the wish for both and the condition that follows, and note how much is usually left out.
Use Chapter 8’s distinction between severities properly and badly used, and the Agathocles verdict that withholds glory.
Take the Remirro de Orco episode as the book’s model of cruelty as theatre: one blow, then the block and knife.
Set the Chapter 17 conditions against the reading: fear without hatred, and hands off property and women.
Conclude on whether the book recommends cruelty or recommends knowing what cruelty is for.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the role of Fortune in The Prince.
essayQuestions.focus: Virtù, fortuna and the limits of control
plan: Begin with the dedication, where the author is himself a victim of fortune’s malignity.
Read Chapter 7 as a case study: Borgia laid every foundation and fell, and the book calls that fortune.
Analyse Chapter 25’s proportion, half and a little less, and the river that can be banked in fair weather.
Weigh the image of fortune as a woman against the premise that men cannot change their natures with the times.
Decide whether the book’s confidence in ability survives its own evidence.

essayQuestions.question: How does Machiavelli argue? Consider his use of examples.
plan: Describe the method announced in Chapter 15: the real truth of the matter rather than the imagination of it.
Show a rule being derived from a case, using Louis XII’s errors in Chapter 3.
Consider the pairing of Borgia and Agathocles, and what the contrast lets the book say.
Test the method on Chapter 19’s Roman emperors, where the examples nearly contradict the rules.
Ask whether argument by example proves anything, or simply makes the conclusion look inevitable.

essayQuestions.question: ‘To all of us this barbarous dominion stinks.’ What difference does the last chapter make to the rest of the book?
plan: Characterise the voice of Chapters 1–25: classifying, cool, without a first-person plural.
Trace Italy through the earlier chapters, in Louis XII’s conquest and the mercenaries’ ruin of the country.
Analyse the shift in Chapter 26: rhetorical questions, a smell, a poem, and a house addressed directly.
Consider what the exhortation implies the rules were for, and whether that redeems or exposes them.
Conclude on whether the book is a treatise with a plea attached or a plea with a treatise in front of it.

discussionQuestions: Machiavelli wrote the book for the family that had imprisoned and tortured him. How should that shape the way we read its advice?
The book allows Agathocles empire but not glory. Is the distinction real, or a way of keeping a respectable conscience while recommending the same methods?
Cesare Borgia did everything right and fell. Does that example strengthen the book’s argument or undermine it?
Is ‘everyone sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are’ a cynical observation or simply an accurate one?
Marriott chose to translate literally rather than smoothly. Where does the roughness of his English seem to serve the argument?

related.why: Shakespeare’s stage Machiavel, a prince who uses the fox and the lion and lets the audience watch him do it.
A conspiracy against a new prince, argued out in advance, and the discovery that killing a ruler settles nothing about who rules.
A king who studies nothing but war and is judged by results; the play tests the book’s advice on a ruler the audience is asked to admire.
A usurper who holds his state by cruelties badly used, renewed and multiplied, exactly as Chapter 8 warns.
Rome’s people and nobles at odds, and a soldier who cannot learn to appear what he is not.
